section_summary: This section spans 1932–1939 and documents Japanese intelligence, espionage, influence operations, and propaganda in China, including approaches to journalists and foreign technical experts. It contains diplomatic reporting on Japanese-controlled propaganda in Wuhan and Canton, with extensive translations of anti-British articles advocating Sino-Japanese cooperation and a Japanese-sponsored “New Order” in East Asia. Other records concern suspected military uses of imported timber, espionage arrests, propaganda about American military assistance to China, and cross-references to related reports and Japanese war literature.

subfiles.title: Document file note: pressure on E. S. Durassoff
subfiles.about: The note cross-references a report about Soviet and Japanese secret-police pressure on an American consular clerk in Harbin.
subfiles.summary: The file note identifies E. S. Durassoff as a clerk at the American Consulate General in Harbin. It refers the reader to file 125.4613/273 for a report concerning pressure applied to him by Soviet and Japanese secret authorities.

subfiles.title: Telegram concerning Japanese purchases of Port Orford cedar
subfiles.about: Prince warns that large Japanese purchases of Port Orford cedar might conceal preparations for mines or another destructive military purpose.
subfiles.summary: O. A. Prince urges serious consideration of heavy Japanese purchases of Port Orford cedar logs during the preceding three years. He reports that the logs were understood to be submerged in Shanghai harbor and speculates that they might camouflage mine-laying, electrical combustion, or another destructive objective.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese liaison officer’s approach to a correspondent
subfiles.about: The note reports an alleged Japanese financial approach to an American newspaper correspondent and a possible similar approach to a League of Nations committee.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese liaison officer allegedly approached an American newspaper correspondent in Shanghai with a financial offer if he would portray events “as they are.” The note adds that the officer was expected to adopt a similar position toward a League of Nations committee traveling to Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Tientsin despatch no. 116
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: Lockhart forwards copies of his despatch no. 116 to the Legation at Beijing.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart transmits copies of a despatch prepared for the American Legation at Beijing. The despatch concerns the alleged capture of Japanese newspaper men and the activities of John N. Meijbroek.

subfiles.title: Alleged Capture of Japanese Newspaper Men
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.about: Lockhart reports an alleged secret mission by John N. Meijbroek to secure the release of four Japanese newspaper men held near Shanhaiguan.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart encloses a letter from E. J. Winans describing Meijbroek’s attempt to obtain help in releasing four Japanese newspaper men reportedly captured by Chinese forces outside the Great Wall. He finds it extraordinary that such a capture had not appeared in the press and notes that Meijbroek spoke Japanese fluently, was married to a Japanese woman, and associated with Japanese residents in Tianjin.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting Meijbroek’s mission
subfiles.about: Winans reports that John N. Meijbroek sought assistance in arranging the release of Japanese newspaper men.
subfiles.summary: Winans states that Meijbroek was attempting to secure the release of Japanese newspaper men said to be held at Luanzhou. The surviving text indicates that money was to be tried first and that the Japanese military might act if the effort failed; it also mentions Meijbroek’s movements along the railway near Tangshan.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Economic Intelligence Commission
subfiles.about: The note describes the South Manchuria Railway Company’s formation of an Economic Intelligence Commission associated with the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: The commission was reportedly organized to consolidate advantages gained by the Japanese Army in Manchuria. The note cross-references the fuller report in file 895.77/2848.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese Information Bureau propaganda
subfiles.about: The note identifies a telegram concerning English-language propaganda issued by the Japanese Information Bureau at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: The file note records that the Japanese Information Bureau was publishing and disseminating news propaganda in English. It directs readers to telegram no. 1321 from China for the examples reproduced on the following pages.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1321: examples of Japanese news propaganda
subfiles.from: American Legation, Peiping, for the Minister by Engert
subfiles.about: The telegram reproduces Japanese propaganda alleging American arms sales and expanding American military influence in China.
subfiles.summary: The first item claims that Zhang Xueliang and Chu Ching Lang purchased American aircraft, antiaircraft guns, machine guns, and trench mortars. The second alleges that Chinese authorities planned to replace German specialists with American instructors in aviation, chemical warfare, poison gas, and smoke-screen training.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese aspersions on foreign intentions
subfiles.about: The note references a despatch reporting Japanese efforts to discredit other nations’ intentions toward China.
subfiles.summary: The note states that Japanese news agencies had expanded their propaganda beyond the Manchurian controversy. They were disseminating claims designed to cast doubt on the motives of other powers toward China.

subfiles.title: Extract from despatch no. 221 on Japanese news propaganda
subfiles.about: The extract lists Japanese allegations that an American wheat loan concealed munitions purchases and that foreign powers were expanding their spheres of influence in China.
subfiles.summary: Japanese agencies reportedly claimed that only a small portion of the American wheat loan would purchase wheat and that the balance would fund munitions. They also accused foreign powers of enlarging their spheres of influence while professing to assist China, including through American support for Chinese aviation.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Chengchow espionage case
subfiles.about: The note identifies a report about three Japanese and one Chinese accused of espionage and fomenting disturbances in Henan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced Chengchow case involved the arrest of four alleged agents. Chinese authorities charged them with conducting espionage for Japan and encouraging unrest in Henan.

subfiles.title: Report extract: Chengchow espionage case
subfiles.about: The extract reports the arrest of three Japanese and one Chinese at Zhengzhou on espionage charges.
subfiles.summary: Chinese authorities arrested the four men on January 5 and seized documents from their premises. The Japanese suspects were transferred the next day to the Japanese consul, while Chinese officials alleged that they had spied for their government and fomented disturbances in Henan.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 490: Enquiry for address of Mr. Leeland Andrus
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, for the Ambassador, Nanking
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports its guarded handling of F. W. Poate Jr.’s request for Leeland Andrus’s address.
subfiles.summary: The despatch encloses Poate’s request, the Embassy’s reply, and a memorandum explaining the reply. Although officials considered Andrus’s suspicions somewhat far-fetched, they honored his request not to disclose his location and reported the matter as potentially significant.

subfiles.title: Letter seeking Leeland Andrus’s address
subfiles.about: Poate asks American officials to locate Leeland Andrus on behalf of a purported sister in Honolulu.
subfiles.summary: Poate says Mrs. McDonough of Honolulu had asked him to find her brother, who arrived at Shanghai in October 1936 to work as a wireless expert and instructor at the Central Aviation School in Nanjing. He reports that letters addressed to Andrus had been returned as unknown and requests a forwarding address.

subfiles.title: Embassy reply to F. W. Poate Jr.
subfiles.from: J. Hall Paxton, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The Embassy tells Poate that Andrus’s wife denied he had a sister of the stated name in Honolulu.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Poate’s inquiry about Mrs. McDonough and Leeland Andrus. Without revealing Andrus’s location, it states that Mrs. Andrus said her husband had no sister of that name living in Honolulu.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation: whereabouts of Leeland Andrus
subfiles.about: Andrus explains why he believes Poate’s inquiry originated with Japanese agents seeking contact with or influence over him.
subfiles.summary: Andrus denied having a sister named McDonough and described Poate as a suspicious British acquaintance from the voyage to China. He said letters had repeatedly been opened, resealed, and sent to him since his arrival in Nanjing, and that Holbrook had been told by Chinese intelligence that such inquiries originated with Japanese agencies. Andrus believed the purpose might be bribery and requested a noncommittal reply that did not reveal his whereabouts.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 504: follow-up on the Andrus inquiry
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, for the Ambassador, Nanking
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards Poate’s response to its earlier handling of his request for Andrus’s address.
subfiles.summary: The despatch refers to no. 490 of June 7 and encloses Poate’s reply dated June 7. It records the conclusion of the exchange without disclosing Andrus’s location.

subfiles.title: Poate’s acknowledgment of the Embassy reply
subfiles.about: Poate accepts that Andrus may have no sister in Honolulu and says he will forward the Embassy’s reply without comment.
subfiles.summary: Poate acknowledges the Embassy’s letter of June 5. He says the explanation is quite possible, apologizes for the trouble, and thanks the Embassy for its courtesy.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese air-dropped posters over Wuhan
subfiles.about: The note cross-references translations of posters dropped by Japanese aircraft during an air raid on Wuhan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report concerns propaganda produced during the Sino-Japanese conflict. Japanese aircraft allegedly dropped the posters over Wuhan, and the reporting officer enclosed translated copies.

subfiles.title: Despatch: Anti-foreign Propaganda
subfiles.from: R. Y. Jarvis, American Consul, Hankow
subfiles.about: Jarvis forwards Japanese-sponsored Wuhan propaganda attacking Western powers, particularly Britain.
subfiles.summary: Jarvis encloses a Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society circular and five translated articles from the Japanese-controlled Wuhan Pao. The material defends Japan’s invasion, attacks Chiang Kai-shek and communism, advocates Sino-Japanese cooperation, and revives charges of white imperialism against Britain, the United States, France, and Russia. Jarvis reports little Chinese response and suggests that Japanese authorities were using puppet organizations to bear responsibility for the campaign.

subfiles.title: Original Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society circular
subfiles.from: Bureau of Social Affairs, Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society
subfiles.about: This is the Chinese original of a Japanese-sponsored circular explaining the occupation and urging peace and cooperation with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The OCR preserves almost none of the Chinese text, but the despatch and succeeding translation identify it as the circular issued on March 28. It accompanied the English translation entitled “What the People of Wuhan Should Hereafter Know.”

subfiles.title: What the People of Wuhan Should Hereafter Know
subfiles.from: Bureau of Social Affairs, Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society
subfiles.about: The circular condemns Chiang Kai-shek, justifies Japan’s invasion, promotes Sino-Japanese cooperation, and appeals for acceptance of the occupation order.
subfiles.summary: The circular presents Chiang Kai-shek’s alliance with Russia, toleration of communism, and resistance to Japan as disastrous errors while accusing Western powers of exploiting China. It portrays Japan’s military expedition as an effort to overthrow a Soviet puppet, eliminate communism, and save both China and Japan rather than conquer Chinese territory. It praises the Peace Maintenance Society for restoring order in Wuhan and urges support for peace, Wang Jingwei, Konoe’s “New Order,” and a Japanese-sponsored government.

subfiles.title: Construction of a New China and Anti-British Movement
subfiles.about: The article depicts British financial support for Chiang Kai-shek as the principal obstruction to peace and calls for action against Britain.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that Chiang’s resistance could soon collapse without foreign assistance and that British loans alone were prolonging the war. It invokes declarations by Japanese-sponsored governments to characterize Britain as an enemy of the Chinese people and a violator of the emerging order. It concludes by endorsing demands to recover concessions, deport British residents, and oppose Great Britain.

subfiles.title: Reminiscences on the Shameen Tragedy
subfiles.about: The article recounts the 1925 Shamian and Shaji violence as historical justification for renewed anti-British agitation.
subfiles.summary: The article links strikes in Hong Kong and Shamian to the May Thirtieth incident in Shanghai and describes the mobilization of workers, students, and civic bodies in Guangzhou. It accuses British forces of machine-gunning demonstrators near Shamian’s West Bridge and emphasizes the resulting deaths, boycott, and disruption of trade between Guangzhou and Hong Kong. The historical narrative is presented in inflammatory language intended to revive hostility toward Britain.

subfiles.title: Historical Facts of British Aggression in China, first installment
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper report of a broadcast
subfiles.from: General Headquarters of the Ta Ming Hui, reprinted by Wuhan Pao
subfiles.about: The broadcast presents a polemical history of British expansion in China from the Opium War through intervention in Tibet.
subfiles.summary: The account begins with Lin Zexu’s destruction of opium and describes the Opium War treaties, treaty ports, indemnities, foreign jurisdiction, the annexation of Burma, and the Boxer settlement as British aggression. It then reviews British competition with Russia and France, leases and railway interests, the Anglo-Japanese alliance, and the British expedition to Lhasa. The article claims Britain fostered Tibetan separatism and portrays its contemporary cooperation with Chiang Kai-shek as a continuing threat.

subfiles.title: Historical Facts of British Aggression in China, second installment
subfiles.about: The article extends its account of alleged British aggression from the early Republic through the contemporary Sino-Japanese War.
subfiles.summary: It alleges that Britain used Yuan Shikai and regional militarists to maintain supremacy and exploited commercial connections between Hong Kong and Guangzhou. It cites the May Thirtieth incident and later violence at Hankou, Jiujiang, Chongqing, Nanjing, Shaji, and Wanxian as evidence of British oppression. The article concludes that British loans enabled Chiang Kai-shek to continue both the war and the killing of Chinese people.

subfiles.title: Anti-British Movement
subfiles.about: The editorial calls for a nationwide anti-British movement in support of the Japanese-sponsored political order.
subfiles.summary: The editorial welcomes anti-British organizations in Nanjing, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, and Kaifeng and presents Britain as the common enemy of Chinese peace and national salvation. It invokes the Opium War, the May Thirtieth movement, and shootings at Hankou and elsewhere to argue that earlier Chinese resistance failed only because it was not sustained. It urges Chinese people to join anti-colonial movements in Burma and India while overthrowing both Chiang Kai-shek and the British interests allegedly directing him.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: anti-foreign propaganda through Japanese puppets
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report on anti-foreign propaganda disseminated through puppet organizations in Japanese-occupied China.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies despatch no. 69 from Jinan to the Embassy at Beijing. The original report was filed under 793.94/15064 rather than with this subject file.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Japanese propaganda at Canton
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Canton report describing the shift of Japanese propaganda toward anti-British themes during the Anglo-Japanese crisis.
subfiles.summary: It notes that propaganda in Guangzhou had previously concentrated on Chiang Kai-shek and communism. As the Anglo-Japanese crisis developed, the campaign became increasingly anti-British and included suggestions that the Japanese Army might act against Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Covering despatch: Japanese Propaganda in Canton
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Myers forwards a copy of his despatch no. 26 to the Embassy at Beijing concerning Japanese propaganda in Guangzhou.
subfiles.summary: The covering letter transmits the substantive report on Japanese propaganda in occupied Guangzhou. It identifies the enclosed document as despatch no. 26, also dated July 19, 1939.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 26: Japanese Propaganda in Canton
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping
subfiles.about: Myers reports the media, themes, and increasing anti-British emphasis of Japanese propaganda in occupied Guangzhou.
subfiles.summary: Since the October 1938 occupation, Japanese-sponsored posters, pamphlets, newspapers, radio broadcasts, and public speeches had attacked Chiang Kai-shek and communism while promoting peace, Sino-Japanese cooperation, and a “New Order in East Asia.” During the Tianjin concession crisis, Japanese-controlled newspapers and station XGOK increasingly invoked earlier British aggression and demanded the removal of British footholds in China. Myers also reports a Japanese Army statement expressing concern about Hong Kong and suggesting that forces in South China were prepared to support pressure on Britain.

subfiles.title: Statement of the Japanese Army Authorities in Canton
subfiles.from: Japanese Army authorities in Canton, published by the Canton Daily Sun
subfiles.about: The statement supports Japanese demands in the Tianjin crisis and warns Britain to abandon its pro-Chiang and allegedly anti-Japanese policies.
subfiles.summary: The garbled clipping says the Tianjin concession issue had moved to negotiations in Tokyo while anti-British movements spread in China and Japan. It accuses British authorities of obstructing Japanese military operations, supporting Chiang Kai-shek, and disturbing plans for a new order in the Far East. The Japanese South China Expeditionary Forces declare themselves prepared to ensure that Britain changes course and cooperates with Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: English translations of Japanese war novels
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a despatch enclosing English translations of the Japanese war novels Mud and Soldiers and Barley and Soldiers.
subfiles.summary: The novels were translated into English by K. Bush and L. W. Bush. The original papers and enclosed copies were filed with despatch no. 4054 under file 793.94/15318.
